title: The Gap Is Not in the Materials
author: The Secondary Literacy Commons
summary: This recap of the October Secondary Literacy Commons session argues that the obstacle to high-quality instructional materials is implementation, not curriculum design. It cites an SRI study finding that more than 70 percent of observed HQIM classrooms were not achieving the robust close reading the materials call for. Luke Morin's answer is text-driven coaching rather than generic professional development, built on curriculum-based professional learning and deliberate practice. The five-step protocol has teacher and coach each prepare the text independently, compare notes, observe or co-teach, and then examine student work together. A live demonstration with Chapter 1 of The Giver shows two independent preps surfacing a better instructional focus than either had alone. The piece closes with how to scale the model when time is short and why belief and culture still decide whether it takes hold.
points: Generic sit-and-get professional development cannot close the gap between a well-designed curriculum and a well-executed lesson, because teachers never practise the actual text with their actual students.
Text-driven coaching makes the curriculum itself the guide, with coach and teacher both doing the intellectual work of reading and drafting a strong student response before they meet.
The step most coaching cycles skip is reviewing student work as the residue of planning decisions, which links what was planned to what students understood.
The minimum viable version is a 20-minute check-in on one paragraph that both people have prepared, which still beats a long observation cycle with no shared prep.
The protocol only works inside a culture where leaders go first, early wins are visible and trying something hard with a coach in the room is normal rather than evaluative.
quotes: Luke’s argument, backed by research on deliberate practice, is that generic PD cannot close the implementation gap. What closes it is coaching that is rooted in the specific text a teacher is about to teach.
The first is curriculum-based professional learning: the curriculum is the guide for all teacher development. Not a general framework. Not a best-practices menu.
Looking at student work as “relics” of instructional decisions is how you build a teacher’s ability to connect what they planned with what students actually did or didn’t understand.
Two smart people reading the same text independently will notice different things. The coaching conversation is where those different noticings become instructional decisions.

A teacher who has deeply engaged with a text before teaching it is a different teacher in the room. They are more alive to student thinking, more able to hear when a student says something unexpected and know whether it’s a misconception or an insight.

A 20-minute check-in on a single paragraph, where both the coach and teacher have read that paragraph and drafted a response, still produces better instruction than a 90-minute observation cycle where neither person has done the text work in advance.
The protocol needs the culture. The culture needs the protocol. They build each other.
